The turbine was designed for an average turbine inlet temperature of 2500°F (2960°R).
The turbine airflow was 4 lb/s, with 3-5% of the total airflow used for rotor blade cooling and 3-5% used for stator blade cooling.
The turbine was designed to have an adiabatic efficiency of 90% total-to-total at the design point.
The turbine work was designed to be 140 BTU/lb.
The turbine had a mean diameter of 12.5 inches and a hub-to-tip ratio of 0.7.
The rotor blade aspect ratio was 1.5.
The cascade testing exposed some blades to average temperatures as high as 2900°F.
The cascade testing ran for a total of 14 hours, including 1.5 hours at an average gas temperature of 2560°F.
The cascade testing found the blades to be in satisfactory condition after the high-temperature exposure.
The analytical thermal predictions were validated by the temperature data obtained during the cascade testing.

The Phase I work concluded that the necessary fabrication techniques, materials, analytical methods, and test facilities were sufficiently advanced to warrant continued development of this high-temperature turbine component.
The turbine design was integrated with a cycle analysis study to evaluate the effects of increased turbine inlet temperature on engine performance.
Increasing the turbine inlet temperature from 2000°F to 2500°F was estimated to more than double the engine horsepower and significantly reduce the specific fuel consumption.
Transpiration cooling was selected as the cooling method for both the stator and rotor blades due to its superior cooling effectiveness at high temperatures.
The preliminary turbine design had a higher than desired rotor exit Mach number of 0.61, which was reduced to 0.48 by increasing the rotor exit area.
